issues.description: The UML/problem statement declares a boolean attribute named 'excellentEnough' in ExcellenceLand, but the solution implementation uses a boolean field named 'isExcellent' with getter isExcellent(). This name mismatch between the specification (excellentEnough) and the implementation (isExcellent) is a structural inconsistency that can confuse students about the exact attribute and getter they must provide (the task explicitly asks for getters for all attributes and references the UML attribute name).
issues.suggestedFix: Make the boolean attribute name in the implementation match the UML/problem statement: rename the field to 'excellentEnough', update the constructor parameter accordingly, and provide the getter isExcellentEnough() (or getExcellentEnough() if preferred consistently). Alternatively, update the problem statement/UML to use 'isExcellent' and document the expected getter name so template, tests, and instructions are consistent.

issues.description: The UML/problem statement defines a boolean attribute named 'excellentEnough' for ExcellenceLand, but the solution (and template placeholder) uses the identifier 'isExcellent' for that concept (field and getter). This naming mismatch between 'excellentEnough' and 'isExcellent' can confuse students trying to map the UML attribute to the implemented field and getter and may cause tests that expect the UML name to fail.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the boolean attribute name with the UML: rename the field and its getter to match 'excellentEnough' (use Java boolean getter convention, e.g. private boolean excellentEnough; public boolean isExcellentEnough()). Alternatively, update the UML/problem statement to reflect the implemented name 'isExcellent' if that was the intended attribute name.
